Housing finance and its consequences for architecture

Irfan Nazar BJK22AR007
Bishop Jerome Institute
B.Arch · Semester 9 · Housing ART 503 · 2026–27

13 October 2026
Research checked 12 October 2026

Presenter notesOpen with the relationship between money and space. A housing proposal needs land, design, approvals, infrastructure and finance. This presentation asks where NHB fits into that process and whether its support produces homes that people can afford and use. Estimated speaking time: 15–18 minutes. The interactive activities are optional during a short classroom slot.
Sources: CASE Irfan Nazar / Housing 01
01 / Introduction

The institution behind
housing lenders

A national development finance institution established by statute

NHB supports the institutions that finance housing in India.

It supplies refinance, supports market development and supervises housing finance companies (HFCs).

Individual homebuyers normally borrow from a bank or HFC. NHB does not make retail home loans directly to individuals.

NHB
Institutional finance
Bank / HFC
Borrower appraisal and home loan
Household
Purchase, construction or improvement

Architectural relevance: access to finance affects which households can occupy a proposed home.

Presenter notesDefine refinance as financing supplied to a lender against eligible loans it has made. HFC means housing finance company. A primary lending institution, or PLI, deals with the household. NHB works mainly through this institutional layer. The distinction matters because NHB refinance eligibility and household loan approval are different decisions. Source detail: Annual Report 2025–26, printed pp.20 and 32–34. The FAQ contains old ownership and regulation wording. Only its statement on the absence of direct individual loans is used here.
Sources: NHB · AR · FAQ Irfan Nazar / Housing 02
02 / Background and need

Why housing needed
an apex institution

Long repayment periods required a stronger institutional finance system

The original gap

The Seventh Plan housing-finance review identified a shortage of long-term finance for individual households.

The institutional response

A national institution could mobilise resources and strengthen dedicated housing lenders across regions.

The housing consequence

Without accessible credit, even a well-designed house can remain beyond a household’s purchasing capacity.

Finance expands purchasing capacity.
Land, services and construction determine what it can purchase.
Presenter notesExplain the difference between a housing need and bankable demand. A family may need a house but lack documented income, clear title or the savings for an initial contribution. NHB’s creation addressed institutional finance constraints. The final statement is architectural analysis: increasing credit alone cannot supply serviced land or guarantee an adequate dwelling. The institution emerged from the Seventh Five Year Plan review, followed by the Rangarajan-led high-level group and the 1987 legislative decision.
Sources: NHB Irfan Nazar / Housing 03
03 / Historical evolution

A changing mandate

Select a milestone to discuss its significance

1987–88

Parliament enacted the NHB Act, 1987. NHB began on 9 July 1988 with RBI ownership.

2007–18

RESIDEX began in 2007. The Affordable Housing Fund followed in 2018.

2019

Government of India acquired RBI’s shareholding. HFC regulation, including registration, moved to RBI on 9 August 2019. NHB retained supervision.

2023–26

NHB manages UIDF and serves as a Central Nodal Agency for PMAY-U 2.0 ISS. Its FY 2025–26 report records continued refinance and supervision.

Presenter notesUse the 2019 milestone to correct a common textbook error. Government ownership and the transfer of regulatory powers are separate changes in the same year. Regulation concerns the rules and registration of HFCs. NHB continues inspections and monitoring, as the latest annual report confirms. Do not describe NHB as the current licensing authority for HFCs. RESIDEX tracks residential prices rather than construction cost or the affordability of every household.
Sources: NHB · MILE · AR Irfan Nazar / Housing 04
04 / Objectives, vision and mission

Inclusion with stability

The mandate combines sector development with financial soundness

Vision, paraphrased

Expand housing finance inclusively while maintaining stability.

Mission, paraphrased

Serve housing needs across the population, with emphasis on households with low and moderate incomes.

Resources

Mobilise funds and channel them towards housing.

Reach

Strengthen institutions serving different regions and income groups.

Affordability

Promote viable, cost-effective housing credit.

Housing supply

Encourage serviced land, materials and improvement of the housing stock.

PMAY-U 2.0 annual household income: EWS up to ₹3 lakh, LIG above ₹3–6 lakh, MIG above ₹6–9 lakh. Limits vary by scheme.

Presenter notesThe vision and mission are paraphrases rather than quotations. Stability matters because a lender that cannot meet its obligations cannot sustain credit delivery. For PMAY-U 2.0, EWS means household annual income up to ₹3 lakh, LIG above ₹3 lakh up to ₹6 lakh, and MIG above ₹6 lakh up to ₹9 lakh. These particular limits belong to that scheme. Other schemes and earlier policies can define the groups differently.
Sources: NHB Irfan Nazar / Housing 05
05 / Institutional structure

Governance and relationships

Government ownership, institutional lending and local implementation

Owner / administrative context

Government of India

Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance

Governance

Board of Directors

Managing Director and executive management

Operations

Head office, New Delhi

16 regional offices as of June 2026, including Thiruvananthapuram

Core work areas

Refinance, project finance, resource mobilisation, supervision, government schemes, research and risk management.

Public agencies

MoHUA and states link policy, subsidy and infrastructure. ULBs and housing agencies deliver projects and services.

Private and social actors

Banks and HFCs lend. Developers build. NGOs can assist mobilisation and documentation. Households repay and occupy.

Presenter notesThis is a functional summary, not a reproduction of every department or the official organisation chart. The Annual Report 2025–26, printed pp.20–25, describes governance and regional presence. National ownership does not remove state and municipal responsibilities for land-use permission, infrastructure and local implementation. NGO involvement is shown as a possible support relationship, not as a formal NHB administrative tier. Households generally connect through PLIs.
Sources: NHB · AR Irfan Nazar / Housing 06
06 / Characteristics and loan features

How NHB’s finance works

Institutional refinance and retail mortgages have different terms

FeatureNHB and the lenderLender and the household
FundsCapital, bonds, money-market borrowing and designated funds. International credit lines support specific initiatives.A PLI combines its funding sources to make home loans.
LendingRefinance against eligible housing-loan portfolios. Project finance supports eligible housing supply.Purchase, construction, extension or repair, subject to appraisal.
Price and repaymentScheme-specific rates and tenures. Fixed or floating options apply. Concessions do not automatically equal retail rate cuts.Contractual interest and monthly instalments. Income, tenure and loan size affect repayment.
Security and accessNHB assesses institutional eligibility, performance and security under its scheme.Property mortgage / title checks and borrower credit appraisal. Required own contribution remains a barrier.

Loans against property for non-housing purposes are excluded from the cited refinance scheme. NHB’s rate is not an individual borrower’s quoted rate.

Presenter notesThe table separates two financing relationships. Avoid presenting one universal NHB rate, collateral rule or tenure. Institutional security may include the relevant statutory security arrangements and scheme documentation. The underlying retail mortgage belongs to the PLI. Refinance can support liquidity, but a PLI still assesses repayment ability and clear title. In the 2024 scheme booklet, loans for furnishing, fees and insurance are also excluded. Resource mobilisation is covered in the latest annual report, printed pp.35–36.
Sources: AR · RF Irfan Nazar / Housing 07
07 / Core role in housing

Finance connects to housing
through several routes

Housing provision includes the dwelling, its services and its long-term use

Housing issueNHB’s contributionArchitectural implication
Urban and rural creditRefinance through eligible PLIs, including banks, HFCs, RRBs and small finance banks.Proposals need realistic household budgets and clear tenure.
Affordable housingAHF and targeted refinance support eligible smaller loans and priority segments.Efficient area planning must preserve habitability.
Housing supplyProject finance provides a supply-side route for eligible agencies and projects.Appraisal requires viable costs, approvals and implementation.
InfrastructureUIDF supports public agencies in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities.Water, sewerage and drainage influence usable housing.
Policy and knowledgeSubsidy administration, RESIDEX, research and capacity building. Green-housing initiatives connect finance to certification.Architects can document costs, performance and scheme compliance.
Presenter notesThis is the core housing slide. Explain that NHB’s influence is usually indirect. It does not choose every plot or design every dwelling. Technology and materials enter through research, capacity building and green-housing support. NHB is not a construction-technology certification agency. Rural housing access also depends on income seasonality, title and the local lender network. UIDF urban services complement housing but its sanctioned projects cannot all be counted as houses.
Sources: AR · UIDF Irfan Nazar / Housing 08
08 / Programmes and initiatives

Different instruments,
different beneficiaries

Each programme has a specific objective and delivery route

Instrument / statusTarget and mechanismImplementation / reported outcome
AHF / currentEligible rural and urban housing loans, with EWS emphasis. NHB refinances PLIs.FY 2025–26: ₹9,100 crore and 52,398 dwelling units.
PMAY-U 2.0 ISS / currentEligible EWS / LIG / MIG homebuyers receive interest subsidy through PLIs.NHB is a CNA. By June 2026: ₹397.42 crore sanctioned for 1.04 lakh beneficiaries.
UIDF / currentPublic agencies deliver eligible infrastructure in Tier 2 / Tier 3 cities. NHB manages the fund.By June 2026: ₹16,852.49 crore sanctioned, ₹2,738.06 crore disbursed.
SUNREF / 2017–22Green affordable housing through a €100m credit line and EU grants, with technical assistance.AFD’s 2025 evaluation assesses results and limits.
Earlier CLSS / historicalInterest subsidy for eligible housing borrowers under earlier PMAY-U rules.EWS/LIG window ended March 2022, MIG March 2021. These are different from ISS.

CNA = Central Nodal Agency. Sanctions, disbursements and completed dwellings measure different stages.

Presenter notesRead one row across as objective, target group, mechanism, implementation and outcome. AHF uses institutional refinance, whereas ISS uses a subsidy credited through a PLI. UIDF supports infrastructure. SUNREF combined credit, investment support and technical assistance. The latest report, printed pp.40–44 and Annexure VIII, supplies the current data. Additional NHB initiatives include fixed-rate refinance, construction refinance, small-ticket rural loans and a slum redevelopment / low-cost housing scheme. RHISS has historically supported eligible rural households outside the relevant PMAY coverage. CRGFTLIH provides credit-risk support to eligible lenders for lower-income housing. Neither a guarantee nor a subsidy means automatic loan approval.
Sources: AR · ISS · EVAL Irfan Nazar / Housing 09
09 / Implementation and affordability

The household’s loan
still needs to be affordable

Refinance, subsidy and repayment are separate mechanisms

1. Household and PLI

The bank / HFC checks income, title, loan purpose and repayment capacity, then lends to the household.

2. PLI and NHB

The eligible lender seeks refinance against qualifying loans. It remains responsible for its retail loan.

3. Subsidy, where eligible

Under ISS, MoHUA funds flow through a CNA such as NHB and the PLI to the beneficiary’s loan account.

ISS: income ≤ ₹9 lakh, loan ≤ ₹25 lakh, house value ≤ ₹35 lakh and carpet area ≤ 120 m². Other eligibility and account conditions apply. Subsidy is 4% on the first ₹8 lakh for up to 12 years, with a maximum release of ₹1.80 lakh in five annual instalments.

Illustrative repayment calculator
₹13,017monthly EMI

43.4% of an illustrative ₹30,000 monthly income

A teaching model with a constant rate. Excludes fees, subsidy and living costs. Rates are assumptions, not an NHB offer.

Presenter notesMove the loan slider from ₹15 lakh to ₹20 lakh while holding the other values constant. This shows why a cheaper rate does not erase the price of land and construction. EMI is P × r × (1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n − 1), with r the monthly rate and n the number of months. The percentage uses a hypothetical monthly household income of ₹30,000, with no assumed universal lending threshold. ISS is not a flat 4% retail loan and the model does not calculate its benefit. MoHUA guidelines, printed pp.23–26, explain ISS and its conditions. Families must meet the housing-ownership and prior-assistance conditions as well.
Sources: RF · ISS Irfan Nazar / Housing 10
10 / Case study context

Happinest Palghar-1

Nandore village, Palghar, Maharashtra

Documented example, 2022

Developer
Mahindra Happinest Developers Ltd

Architect
Ashok B Lall Architects

849dwelling units
8.35acres of site

11 residential buildings, ground + 4 floors. Compact 1RK, 1BHK and 2BHK homes address the LIG market.

Launched February 2018. IGBC Green Affordable Housing pre-certification: Platinum, as documented in the booklet.

NHB documented this SUNREF learning example. A direct NHB construction loan is not established.

Presenter notesUse this case to connect finance policy and architectural choices. The diagram is the source’s developer rendering and should not be called a site survey or as-built plan. The developer’s 2018 results verify the launch month. The 2022 booklet documents its features and HDFC as a retail lender. Do not assert an NHB project-finance amount. Some fields in the booklet’s p.50 date table are misaligned, so they are not used. The case concerns the documented project scope, not every later phase under the same brand.
Sources: CASE · ML Irfan Nazar / Housing 11
11 / Case study analysis

Compact homes and
shared environmental services

Architectural lessons from the documented Palghar example

Planning

Shared open space and common facilities support community use. Compact apartments reduce the entry price.

Construction

RCC structure, cementitious material substitution and lightweight block walls. The source varies in its block specification.

Services

Rainwater harvesting, treated-water reuse, efficient fixtures and common-area lighting.

Comfort

The booklet reports daylight and openings to the exterior. Maintenance and actual thermal comfort still need verification.

Finance and social reading

Retail credit connects the buyer to the unit. Interviews highlighted price, layout and developer credibility.

Compact homes need adequate storage and adaptable layouts. Shared systems require funded maintenance.

Design savings and pre-certification need verification after occupation. These observations are architectural analysis.

Lower initial cost can improve access. Inadequate space or high transport and maintenance costs can reduce the benefit over time.

Presenter notesKeep a critical tone. The case source describes green measures and buyer interviews, but those do not prove reduced bills for every resident. The source describes AAC blocks in one section and CLC blocks in the detailed envelope specification. Do not select one as verified without project drawings. The lesson for an architect is to coordinate an affordable unit with common services, accessible circulation and a maintenance plan. The discussion answer is an interpretation rather than a measured project outcome.
Sources: CASE Irfan Nazar / Housing 12

Presenter notesPoint to the difference between a flow and a stock. Disbursement is money released during a year. Outstanding is the balance still owed at a date. Cumulative refinance is a historical sum and is not the number of distinct homes constructed. The latest annual report gives exact AHF units in Annexure VIII. HFCs received about 80.4% of the year’s refinance. The financing network is an achievement, but social and architectural outcomes require additional evidence.

13 / Limitations and challenges

Credit access remains uneven

The barriers extend beyond the availability of institutional funds

ConstraintEffect on housing accessWhat would help
Informal or irregular incomeA household can need housing yet fail a lender’s repayment assessment.Better income assessment and suitable products, with responsible lending.
Title and own contributionUnclear tenure or limited savings can prevent a mortgage.Tenure support and coordination with land and housing agencies.
Land and service costsHigher land prices can absorb the benefit of cheaper finance.Serviced sites, realistic project costs and infrastructure delivery.
Lender incentivesRefinance concessions may not reach the borrower in full.Track final loan pricing and beneficiary outcomes.
Housing quality and locationPeripheral housing can add transport costs and weaken access to work.Assess location, habitability, maintenance and total living costs.

Analytical assessment. NHB can support finance and institutions, while land policy and local implementation require other agencies.

Presenter notesSeparate the strength of an institution from the limits of its instrument. A larger refinance portfolio can coexist with exclusion. For sustainability, consider energy and water systems alongside access to jobs and everyday services. Administrative challenges include coordination, reliable documentation and monitoring. Financial challenges include repayment risk and interest-rate movements. The independent SUNREF evaluation gives a concrete example of weak borrower pass-through and monitoring, discussed on slide 16.
Sources: RF · EVAL · ISS Irfan Nazar / Housing 14
14 / Relevance to architecture

The architect’s contribution

Housing quality and financial viability need to be considered together

A viable project needs a household budget and a life beyond handover.

At concept stage, connect unit area, sale price and the intended residents’ ability to pay.

During design, make space for infrastructure and maintenance access. Avoid reducing cost through inadequate daylight, ventilation or essential services.

Before appraisal

DPR, cost estimate, title and approval status, phasing and demand assumptions.

In the design

Carpet area, accessible circulation, climate response and appropriate materials.

At handover

Completion evidence, operating instructions and responsibilities for shared systems.

After occupation

Occupancy, actual bills, thermal comfort and resident feedback.

NHB’s programmes give architects a reason to document affordability and performance, alongside form and construction.

Presenter notesThese are professional implications, not a list of compulsory NHB submission documents for every scheme. DPR means detailed project report. Scheme compliance depends on the selected programme, approvals and applicable local requirements. Explain lifecycle affordability using construction cost, EMI, utility bills, maintenance and transport. A specification for efficient equipment should include how residents or the association can maintain and replace it. Technology should fit local capability and budget.
Sources: ISS · CASE · AR Irfan Nazar / Housing 15
15 / Critical analysis

SUNREF’s evaluation
tests the success claim

AFD / ECORYS, April 2025: green affordable housing, 2017–22

57%

EWS / LIG participation

54%

Female ownership

2.4%

Beneficiaries with verified interest-rate subvention under the evaluator’s test

An inclusive intention

The programme joined environmental and affordability objectives. The evaluator found that participation figures largely reflected existing market patterns.

A limited transmission

Disbursement concentrated in two PLIs. Borrowing rates became uncompetitive after COVID-related rate reductions.

An attribution problem

Many homes already existed before refinance. Environmental claims used estimates, with no continuing performance verification.

Programme findings cannot be treated as measured results for Happinest Palghar-1.

Assessment: verify borrower savings and building performance, while widening lender participation.

Presenter notesThis is the strongest evidence-based critical slide. AFD’s project evaluation distinguishes activities from attributable effects. The programme achieved revised participation targets, but that does not show the programme caused those patterns. Its environmental claim was difficult to attribute because properties already existed. The 2.4% measure relates to the evaluation’s applicable interest-rate cap, not to all forms of support. The concluding assessment follows the evaluator’s recommendations for market-sensitive financial design, coordination and measured outcomes. Avoid applying the programme percentages to the Palghar project.
Sources: EVAL · AFD Irfan Nazar / Housing 16
16 / Conclusion

NHB’s value depends on
what finance delivers

A critical conclusion

NHB strengthens the supply of housing finance.
Its social value depends on whether that finance reaches underserved households and supports adequate homes.

Refinance and subsidy need clear borrower benefits. Infrastructure and land policy need coordinated delivery.

For architects, affordability includes usable space, location, services and the cost of living in the home.

Classroom check

Who holds HFC regulatory powers, including registration, after the 2019 transfer?

Answer: RBI. NHB continues HFC supervision, financing and development.

Presenter notesClose with a judgement, not a repeat of the definition. NHB is necessary to housing-finance infrastructure, but finance should be evaluated against its effects on residents. The practical professional response is to connect financing eligibility and cost control to quality, location and post-occupancy evidence. Use the check question only if time permits. A likely viva question is whether NHB can solve the housing shortage by itself. Answer that it works through a wider system of lenders, governments, public agencies and developers.
Sources: AR · RBI · EVAL Irfan Nazar / Housing 17
